# Agents and permissions

## Agent definitions

A durable agent definition is a DB-stored record (`AgentDefinition` in
`swage-storage`) that gives a session its character. Each definition carries:

| Field | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `id` | Stable agent id; sessions carry it as `sessions.agent_id` |
| `topic_id` | `None` = global; `Some(uuid)` = topic-scoped, shadows a global definition with the same id within that topic |
| `display_name` | Human-readable label |
| `description` | Free-text description |
| `instructions` | Appended after operator instructions (never precede them); replaces outright when operator instructions are empty |
| `model_id` | Model preference; applied only when the model id exists in `config.models.entries`, otherwise ignored with a warning |
| `tool_permissions` | Optional JSON overlay (serialised `ToolPermissionConfig`); intersects with the resolved config's grants — narrows, never widens |
| `skills` | Skill ids this definition activates |
| `output_schema` | Optional JSON Schema enforced on every final response |
| `output_max_retries` | Override for schema-validation retry limit |

### Overlay onto the config cascade

`apply_agent_definition` (in `turn/configuration.rs`) overlays a definition
onto the session's resolved file config (Global → Topic → Agent `.toml`
files). The overlay:

1. Appends instructions after operator instructions.
2. Sets the default model if the id is present in `config.models.entries`.
3. Intersects tool permissions via `intersect_tool_permissions` — allow sets
   are intersected, deny sets are unioned. A malformed overlay is logged and
   ignored (the config's own grants stand).
4. Sets `declared_skills` and, when present, `output_schema` and
   `output_max_retries`.

## Effort

Reasoning effort is a single provider-neutral vocabulary of seven levels,
ordered lowest to highest:

| Level | Wire spelling |
|---|---|
| Off | `off` |
| Minimal | `minimal` |
| Low | `low` |
| Medium | `medium` |
| High | `high` |
| Xhigh | `xhigh` |
| Max | `max` |

### Where effort is set

Effort resolves through a three-step fallback:

1. **Per-turn override** — an explicit `effort_override` passed by the
   caller (workflow dispatches, delegated turns).
2. **Session metadata** — set at session creation via the `effort` field
   of `CreateConversationRequest`. Stored in the session's metadata JSON
   and read back on each turn.
3. **Model default** — `default_effort` on the model's catalogue entry
   (`ModelEndpointConfig` in config, `ModelSettings` on the wire). When
   set, every turn using that model inherits the default unless
   overridden above.

When none of these supplies a value, the turn sends no effort control.

The web UI's Settings → Providers panel exposes a **Default effort**
dropdown on each model entry, with all seven levels plus "No effort".
This sets `default_effort` on the model's config entry.

Config example:

```toml
[models.entries.sonnet]
provider_id = "anthropic"
model_id = "claude-sonnet-5"
default_effort = "high"
```

### Resolution

Each model declares an `EffortCapability` — either through the catalogue
entry's `capabilities.effort` field (config or wire), or through the
provider adapter's built-in declaration for models it serves. Three
capability shapes:

| Shape | Fields | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| `Levels` | `levels: [Effort]`, `can_disable: bool` | The control takes named levels from a fixed set. `can_disable` governs whether `off` sends the model's own disable or clamps to the lowest supported level. |
| `Budget` | `min_tokens: u32`, `max_tokens: u32`, `can_disable: bool` | The control takes a numeric thinking budget. The six non-off levels spread monotonically across the declared range. |
| `None` | — | No effort control; every intent is omitted from the request. |

`resolve_effort` (`swage-core/src/effort.rs`) is the single resolution
point. Rules:

- A level the model supports natively passes through.
- An unsupported level clamps to the nearest supported level below the
  request, or to the lowest supported level when nothing lower exists.
- `off` sends the model's disable when `can_disable` is true; otherwise
  clamps to the lowest level with a note.
- A budget model receives a monotone budget across its range (higher
  intent never resolves to a smaller budget).
- A model declaring `None` has the control omitted entirely.

A capability that cannot be honoured (empty levels, inverted budget
range) is refused at config validation (`EffortCapability::validate`),
not at resolution time.

### Adapter declarations

The built-in adapters declare:

| Adapter | Capability |
|---|---|
| Anthropic | Levels: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `max`; `can_disable: true` (Claude models only; non-Claude models return `None`) |
| Chat Completions (OpenAI) | Levels: `minimal`, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`; `can_disable: true` (reasoning models only; non-reasoning models return `None`) |
| Responses (OpenAI) | Same as Chat Completions |
| Google | Budget: Gemini 2.5 Flash `1`–`24576` tokens, Flash Lite `512`–`24576` tokens; `can_disable: true`. Non-Flash Google models return `None`. |
| Codex | Levels: `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`; `can_disable: false` (GPT-5.x models only; others return `None`) |

A catalogue entry's `capabilities.effort` overrides the adapter's
declaration for that model.

### Audit trail

The turn's assembly report records the resolution under
`provider_visible.effort` as a `ResolvedEffort`:

```json
{
  "requested": "max",
  "control": { "kind": "level", "level": "xhigh" },
  "clamped_to": "xhigh",
  "note": "max unsupported; clamped to xhigh"
}
```

When the request was honoured as-is, `clamped_to` and `note` are absent.
This data is stored in the assembly report JSON and available through
`GET /api/turns/{id}/context`; the web UI's context inspector panel
does not yet render it.

## Effective agent registry

A fresh installation's effective agent registry holds one entry: the
shipped default (`"gateway"`, display name "Swage default"). No other
agent definitions ship with the gateway. The start-conversation picker
lists this default plus any operator-authored definitions visible to
the topic (via `GET /api/topics/{topicId}/agent-definitions`).
`CreateConversationRequest`'s `agent_id` field selects one of these:
`"gateway"` or an operator-authored definition visible to the target
topic; the gateway rejects anything else with a validation error.

A shipped workflow's roles (the research sweep's researcher, organiser,
and synthesist) are bare dispatches inside the workflow script, not
standalone agent definitions — they do not appear in the registry or the
picker.

## Operator guidance (`AGENTS.md`)

Operator-authored guidance is a second instruction source, parallel to the
`instructions/` directory. A file named `AGENTS.md` at the root of a
guidance directory is read, and its content enters every turn as an
instruction rule in the prompts element.

### Where it is read from

Two kinds of root are checked, in this order:

1. **Config root** (`~/.swage/` or `$SWAGE_HOME`) — always read. The
   resulting rule carries the `Global` provenance level.
2. **Trusted, readable workspace roots** — the active workspace and any
   workspace attachments that are both trusted and readable. Each produces
   a rule at the `Topic` provenance level.

A workspace root that is not trusted, or that is trusted but not readable
(e.g. a write-only attachment), contributes nothing: workspace content
enters the model's instructions only when both conditions are met. There is
no config knob to disable global guidance — an `AGENTS.md` at the config
root is always read.

### Ordering and layering

Global guidance appears before workspace guidance, so workspace rules
refine the operator's baseline rather than the reverse. Both layers append
after the resolved instruction baseline (the merged `instructions/`
content), extending it without replacing it. Agent-definition instructions
then append after operator guidance, preserving the full chain:
resolved instructions → operator guidance → agent-definition instructions.

### Error handling

An absent `AGENTS.md` is silently skipped — a root without a guidance file
simply contributes nothing. A path that exists but is not a regular file
(e.g. a directory named `AGENTS.md`) is treated the same way. An
unreadable or non-UTF-8 file is logged as a warning and skipped — guidance
never fails a turn.

### Code path

Both foreground and delegated turns call `operator_guidance_rules`
(in `turn/operator_guidance.rs`), which reads the config root's guidance
file then each trusted, readable workspace root's, and returns the ordered rule vec.
The reading itself is in `swage_config::agent_guidance::read_agent_guidance`.
The rules are passed to `build_assembly_elements` (in `turn/context.rs`),
which appends them after the resolved-instructions rule so the
`PromptsElement` emits them in the correct order.

### Visibility in the context inspector

The turn context inspector's prompts element shows the provenance of each
rule by hierarchy level — e.g. `prompt rules (3 total: 1 Global, 2 Topic)`.
Operator guidance rules from the config root appear as `Global`; those from
workspace roots appear as `Topic`.

## Tool permission model

### Permission bypass

`dangerously_skip_permissions = true` is a top-level escape hatch from this
permission model, not another layer within it. If either the session-resolved
configuration or the gateway's startup configuration enables it,
`build_permission_config` returns wildcard allow with no denies or approval
requirements. The turn also pre-approves all remaining tool, location, and
hook gates, including out-of-workspace location prompts. The resolution rules
below apply only while this setting is false in both configurations.

### Resolution order

`check_permission` (`swage-tool/src/permission.rs`) evaluates in strict
order:

1. **Deny wins.** If the tool is in `deny`, return `PermissionDenied(ExplicitlyDenied)`.
2. **Allow gate.** The tool must match the `allow` list — by direct name,
   `"*"` wildcard, or bundle expansion. No match → `PermissionDenied(NotAllowed)`.
3. **Approval check.** If the tool matches a `require_approval` entry
   (direct or bundle-expanded), return `RequiresApproval` with optional
   per-entry `timeout_secs` and `timeout_policy` overrides.
4. **Allow.** Return `Allowed`.

`require_approval` entries never grant access — they only gate tools already
in the allow set. An entry for a tool outside `allow` is inert.

### Defaults

The file-config default (`ToolPermissionConfig::default()` in
`swage-config/src/model.rs`) is:

- `allow: ["*"]` — all tools permitted
- `deny: []`
- Eight high-risk tools gated behind `require_approval`:
  `shell`, `file_edit`, `file_write`, `python_execute`, `browser_click`,
  `browser_type`, `browser_select`, `browser_scroll`
- Default bundles: `browsing`, `browser_actions`, `scheduling`,
  `knowledge-read`, `knowledge-write`, `knowledge-curation`,
  `knowledge-citation`, `knowledge-orientation-curation`

### Effect of a restricted allow list

When an agent definition sets `allow: ["tool_a", "tool_b"]`, the overlay
intersects with the config's default `["*"]`. Since `*` on the config side
defers to the overlay, the effective allow becomes `["tool_a", "tool_b"]`.
The default `require_approval` entries for `shell`, `file_edit`, etc. remain
in the config but are inert: `check_permission` rejects those tools at the
allow gate (step 2) before reaching the approval check (step 3). Setting
`allow: []` yields zero permitted tools.

## Dispatch-bound grant intersection

When an agent delegates a child, the child's effective permissions are the
intersection of its own config and every ancestor dispatcher's grants.

### Lineage

`GatewayDelegationHandler.handle_delegation` (in `turn/delegation.rs`):

1. Loads the target agent's file config and overlays its durable definition
   (`apply_agent_definition`).
2. Fetches the sender's dispatch-bound lineage from session metadata
   (`dispatch_bound_agent_ids`), then appends the sender's own agent id.
3. Calls `apply_dispatch_bounds` with the full lineage — each ancestor's
   resolved config (file config + its own definition) is loaded and applied
   in order via `apply_dispatch_bound`.
4. Stores the lineage in the child's session metadata so further delegation
   continues to narrow.

### Intersection mechanics

`apply_dispatch_bound` (`turn/configuration.rs`) operates on **expanded**
allow sets (bundles resolved to concrete tool names before intersecting,
preventing a shared bundle label from smuggling a wider definition):

1. **Allow intersection.** Both worker and bound allow lists are expanded
   through their respective bundles. Set-intersection produces the effective
   allow. Wildcard on either side defers to the other.
2. **Deny union.** The bound's denies are appended.
3. **Worker approval pruning.** The worker's own `require_approval` entries
   are explicitly filtered to only tools in the effective allow set — unlike
   the agent-definition overlay, where inert entries simply remain.
4. **Bound approval carry-forward.** The bound's `require_approval` entries
   are expanded through the bound's own bundles and carried onto the worker
   for any tool that is (a) in the effective allow set and (b) not already
   approval-gated by the worker. Carried entries use the worker's own
   timeout defaults.

### Audit record

`effective_tool_permissions_record` produces a JSON object with all bundle
labels expanded to concrete tool names:

```json
{ "allow": [...], "deny": [...], "require_approval": [...] }
```

This record is attached to the delegated assembly report
(`DelegatedAssembly.report`) and emitted via the `ContextAssembled` server
event for audit and inspection. It is not injected into the child's model
context — enforcement is handled at the dispatch/permission seam via
`check_permission`, not via prompt text.

## Topic-targeted session creation

`CreateConversationRequest` (`swage-protocol/src/client/conversation.rs`)
carries `#[serde(deny_unknown_fields)]`. Its only fields are
`selected_model_id` and `agent_id` (both optional). Any unrecognised field —
including `topic_id` — is rejected at deserialisation as a 422 error. This
is a structural guarantee from `deny_unknown_fields`, not a
topic_id-specific validation.

Topic-targeted creation uses a separate path-based endpoint:

```
POST /api/topics/{topic_id}/sessions
```

The handler (`create_topic_session` in `handlers.rs`) accepts the same
`CreateConversationRequest` body (or no body) and creates the session
directly in the named topic, returning 201 on success or 404 if the topic is
not found.

## Sandbox and approval flow

### Sandbox isolation

Local tool calls that are eligible for sandboxed execution run inside a
two-layer sandbox (`swage-sandbox`):

1. **Bubblewrap (bwrap)** — Linux namespace isolation (PID, network, mount,
   user, IPC, UTS). `--unshare-all` with `--die-with-parent`. Read-only
   root bind with read-write overlays for the working directory and
   configured mounts.
2. **Landlock** — kernel-enforced per-path filesystem access control,
   applied inside the child process. Supports ABI 1 (Linux 5.13+), ABI 2
   (5.19+, adds `REFER`), ABI 3 (6.2+, adds `TRUNCATE`). Degrades
   gracefully on older kernels. Read-only system paths: `/bin`, `/lib`,
   `/lib64`, `/usr/bin`, `/usr/lib`, `/usr/lib64`, `/etc/ld.so.cache`.
   Always-writable paths: the working directory and `/tmp`, plus any
   configured write paths. Restrictions are irrevocable within the process.

The execution boundary is selected before this sandbox path. When a session
targets a non-local device, tool calls go to that device. On a local device,
tools that require gateway state or host facilities execute directly in the
gateway process; tools with resolved secret parameters also stay on the host
so their raw values do not cross sandbox IPC. These host/device executions
are not confined by the bubblewrap and Landlock layers described here.

Credential isolation strips `OPENAI_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, and
`GOOGLE_API_KEY` from the sandbox child environment. Provider
`api_key_env` names are configurable, however, and any differently named
environment variable is not stripped by this mechanism. LLM completions use
the host IPC proxy, so the child does not need provider credentials for
completion requests.

### Sandbox configuration

| Option | Type | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `sandbox.enabled` | bool | `true` |
| `sandbox.allow_degraded_execution` | bool | `false` |

Setting `sandbox.enabled = false` does not by itself disable sandboxing —
it tells the dispatcher to skip sandbox setup, which counts as degraded
execution. The dispatcher requires the explicit opt-in
`sandbox.allow_degraded_execution = true` before it will proceed without a
sandbox. Without that opt-in, dispatcher construction fails with
`SandboxError::Unavailable`. To run unsandboxed, set both:

```toml
[sandbox]
enabled = false
allow_degraded_execution = true
```

When `enabled` is true and sandbox setup fails at runtime, the recovery
path depends on the turn's attendance:

- **Attended turns** (interactive client connected) — the turn pauses with an
  approval prompt asking whether to proceed unsandboxed. The client may
  approve (the turn retries with degraded execution), reject (the turn is
  marked Failed), or the prompt may time out or be interrupted.
- **Unattended or delegated turns** — the turn is blocked and marked Failed.
  The degradation is recorded in the audit trail via an
  `execution_isolation_degraded` event.

`allow_degraded_execution = true` also opts in to unsandboxed execution
without the approval prompt when sandbox setup fails at runtime, for both
attended and unattended turns. The degradation is recorded in the audit
trail regardless of how it was authorised.

### Approval channel

When `check_permission` returns `RequiresApproval`, the turn pauses and
sends an `ApprovalRequest` to the connected client. The client responds with
a decision (`Approved` or `Rejected`) and a scope.

**Scopes** (`ApprovalDecisionScope`):

| Scope | Persistence | Reach |
|---|---|---|
| `Once` | None — applies to the single pending call | This call only |
| `Session` | In-memory `session_approval_grants`, until the gateway exits | Any session in this gateway process |
| `Permanent` | In-memory + persisted to disk | This topic while the gateway runs; after restart, subject to agent-level `require_approval` configuration |
| `PermanentGlobal` | In-memory + persisted to disk across all topics | All topics while the gateway runs; after restart, subject to topic- and agent-level `require_approval` configuration |

`Session` is process-scoped, not session-scoped, despite the name.
`ApprovalGrantKey` carries no session identifier, and `from_approval` sets
`topic_id: None` for tool and hook approvals, so the grant is stored under a
global key. `build_permission_config` drops the matching `require_approval`
entry whenever that key is present, for every dispatcher built afterwards —
in any session, any topic, until the gateway process exits. Existing
dispatchers keep their original config; the grant takes effect on the next
one built.

For tool approvals, the persisted reach in the table is conditional after a
restart. Persistence removes the tool from `require_approval` in the topic or
global TOML file. That field uses replacement semantics in the Global → Topic
→ Agent cascade, so an agent file can replace a persisted topic list, and a
topic or agent file can replace a persisted global list. The process-local
grant masks such a narrower approval requirement until the gateway exits;
after restart, the narrower configuration takes effect again.

`Permanent` and `PermanentGlobal` also handle location-scoped approvals
(workspace attachment trust). For tool and location approvals alike,
`Permanent` grants carry the approving topic's `topic_id`, while
`PermanentGlobal` grants use `topic_id: None`. `Session` grants are also
global: tool and hook approvals get `topic_id: None` from `from_approval`,
and location approvals explicitly use a global location key.

### Timeout and rejection

| Setting | Default | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `hitl.timeout` | `300` seconds (5 minutes) | `HitlConfig::default()` |
| `hitl.timeout_policy` | `Reject` | `HitlConfig::default()` |

Per-tool overrides via `RequireApprovalEntry::WithOptions { timeout, timeout_policy }`.

**Timeout policies:**

- `Reject` — treat timeout as rejection; the agent receives feedback and the
  turn continues.
- `Interrupt` — mark the turn as Interrupted; no further tool calls or
  completions are issued.

## Context configuration

The `[context]` section of the configuration cascade (Global → Topic → Agent
`.toml` files) governs context assembly and compaction.

| Key | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `assembly` | string | `"default"` | Named context assembly to use |
| `alternatives` | array of strings | `[]` | Named assemblies registered as hidden alternatives; selection records the chosen name locally |
| `timeout` | integer (1–60) | `5` | Assembly timeout in seconds |
| `budget` | integer or absent | absent | Context token budget; must be positive when set |
| `compaction_threshold` | `{ messages = N }` or `{ tokens = N }`, or absent | absent (100 messages) | Size past which a turn's context is compacted; `N` must be positive |
| `diagnosis_reader_model` | string or absent | absent (session's own model) | Model entry or alias for the diagnosis readers during wall succession |
| `diagnosis_synthesis_model` | string or absent | absent (session's own model) | Model entry or alias for the diagnosis synthesis during wall succession |

Every key cascades: a topic file overrides the global, an agent file overrides
the topic. Settings saves reject an invalid `compaction_threshold` (non-positive
count) and a `diagnosis_reader_model` or `diagnosis_synthesis_model` that names
neither a model entry nor an alias in the configuration being saved.

## Voice configuration

The `[voice]` section configures speech transcription and synthesis.

| Key | Type | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| `transcription_model` | string or absent | absent | Model id sent to the default provider's `/audio/transcriptions` endpoint |
| `speech_model` | string or absent | absent | Model id sent to the default provider's `/audio/speech` endpoint |

Voice uses the default provider's OpenAI-protocol audio endpoints. It never
uses the chat model. With a model unset, that capability reports itself
unavailable — `GET /api/voice/capabilities` returns an `unavailable_reason`
naming what to configure
(see [Interfaces and tooling — Voice capabilities](interfaces-and-tooling.md#voice-capabilities)).

Config example:

```toml
[voice]
transcription_model = "whisper-1"
speech_model = "tts-1"
```

Both ids can be edited in the web UI under **Settings → Voice**; a save
applies without a gateway restart.

## Succession compaction

When a turn's assembled message list exceeds the configured
`compaction_threshold` (default: 100 messages), the turn runs on a successor:
the older part of the conversation history is replaced by a summary, the newer
part is kept verbatim, and every other context element — orientation, norms,
prompts, briefings, skills — is rendered afresh from its sources.

### Wall-triggered succession

A session that keeps hitting walls continues on a successor built from a blind
diagnosis, regardless of the context's size. Two triggers are checked within the
6 most recent finished turns:

- 3 failures of the identical tool call (same tool, same arguments) anywhere in
  that window, or
- at least 5 failed tool calls and failed turns combined.

The first trigger is checked first; when both are present, the repeated-call
signal is reported.

The successor carries diagnosis notes in place of the summarised history. Each
turn runs on such a successor while the walls remain among its recent turns:

- **Reuse:** a turn whose recent walls match the set its predecessor's
  diagnosis answered carries that diagnosis again rather than writing a new
  one.
- **Restoration:** a turn with no wall left in the recent window gets its full
  history back.

The diagnosis readers and the synthesis are selected by model catalogue entry
or alias, resolved as ordinary turns resolve a model. When unset, the session's
own model is used.

If any diagnosis reader or the synthesis fails or returns an empty report, the
turn falls back to threshold-only compaction and compacts only when its context
exceeds the threshold.

Transient provider failures — rate limits, timeouts, HTTP 5xx responses,
malformed streams, and connection errors — do not trigger wall succession.
Provider refusals of the agent's request count as walls.

The compaction record carries strategy `succession-degradation` and includes a
diagnosis record with the walls answered and each model call's stage, model,
usage, report, and any failure reason. A reused diagnosis names the turn it
was originally written for. The assembly report retains compaction decisions
from the first assembly and the successor in pass order, even when their names
match.


<!-- source: agent-docs/first-session.md -->

# First session

After the gateway is running and a provider is configured (README), a
first session needs nothing else. A topic, an attached workspace and trust
in it are optional — they give agents their own memory, file access and
project guidance, but a conversation can start without any of them.

## The front door

The web UI opens to the recent-sessions list (`GET /api/sessions`): every
scope's sessions ordered by their latest user or assistant message, with
each entry's preview showing the latest user or assistant message (tool and
system messages never replace the preview). Automated sessions are grouped
beneath their source (`entries[].automated` under a `conversation`,
`schedule` or `workflow_run` source). `?topic_id=`
narrows the list to a topic; `?archived=` (boolean) lists the sessions the
inactivity sweep has hidden (`[sessions] archive_after_days`, default 7;
a turn on an archived session unarchives it). Every session records its
origin (`direct`, `schedule_run`, `workflow_worker`, `delegation`).
Selecting an entry resumes it (`/conversations/{id}`, or
`/conversations/{id}/surfaces/{surface_id}` with a surface open).

Beneath the list, the **New session** control takes a topic (or none) and
an agent, then **Start** opens the composer in that scope. Nothing is
created until the first message: the composer's send creates the
conversation (`POST /api/topics/{topic_id}/sessions`, or
`POST /api/conversations` for the general scope) and then sends. A start
abandoned before the first message leaves no session behind. **+ New
topic** creates a topic (`POST /api/topics`) without starting a session.

## Topics

A topic is optional shared context — memory, knowledge base, attached
workspaces, configuration — for the sessions started in it. A session
started without one runs in the general scope: general memory, the general
knowledge base, no inherited files or context from any topic, and no
`topic_id` on the wire. `GET /api/topics` never lists the general scope,
and it cannot be opened or deleted. Schedules can run in the general scope:
a schedule created without a topic resolves to the general scope.

A session without a topic sees a built-in orientation element at every
turn, describing its environment: no topic is selected, general memory and
the general knowledge base are in scope, and tool paths resolve at a
scratch directory for the session
(`scratch/general/sessions/<session_id>` under the data root). A session
in a topic whose workspace is attached sees its working directory instead;
the scratch layout for topic sessions is
`scratch/topics/<topic>/sessions/<session_id>`.

The top bar names the session's scope; a topic's name links to its settings
page (`/settings/topic/{slug}/{overview|workspaces|surfaces|sessions}`),
where its description, workspaces, default surfaces, tags and sessions are
managed. Every topic is also listed in the settings section navigation.

## Attach a workspace

Open the topic's settings page and select its **Workspaces** tab.

The workspace form takes a filesystem path to an existing repository
directory. The gateway canonicalises whatever it receives, so a relative
path resolves against the gateway process's working directory — use an
absolute path to avoid ambiguity. **Allow file changes** defaults on;
**Trust this workspace** defaults off. Select the access and trust choices,
then **Attach workspace**. The first attachment becomes the default working
folder once trusted, for conversations without an explicit workspace selection.

The attachment appears with its trust state and configured access mode:
read and write access by default, with trust disabled unless selected.
The access mode describes the permissions that take effect once trusted.
While untrusted, the attachment grants no file access and does not
load its `AGENTS.md`.

## Trust the workspace

Unless trusted during attachment, a newly attached workspace is untrusted.
An untrusted workspace contributes nothing — no file access grants and no guidance. Its `AGENTS.md` is not
read into agent context until the workspace is trusted.

Select **Trust workspace** on an untrusted attachment. Its configured file
permissions become active, and the workspace's `AGENTS.md` feeds the agent context for sessions in this
topic.

See [Agents and permissions — Operator guidance](agents-and-permissions.md#operator-guidance-agentsmd)
for how trusted workspace guidance layers into the instruction chain
(global `AGENTS.md` → workspace `AGENTS.md` → agent-definition
instructions).

## Start a conversation with a chosen agent

The agent picker — on the front door's **New session** control, and in the
composer until the first message — lists the scope's effective agent
definitions: the shipped default (`"gateway"`, display name **Swage
default**) plus any operator-authored definitions visible to the topic, or
the global ones for the general scope. Selecting an agent and submitting the
first message creates a conversation bound to that definition and navigates
to it immediately.

The picker queries `GET /api/topics/{topicId}/agent-definitions`, or
`GET /api/agent-definitions` for the general scope. The `agent_id` field of
`CreateConversationRequest` carries the selection; omitting it uses the
default. Every conversation read (`ConversationResponse`,
`ConversationSummary`, `ConversationDetail`) carries the `agent_id` the
session runs under. See
[Agents and permissions — Effective agent registry](agents-and-permissions.md#effective-agent-registry)
for what the registry contains and how definitions shadow.

## Revoke trust and detach

**Revoke trust** marks the workspace untrusted — its file grants and
guidance are removed from future turns without changing its configured access mode. **Detach** removes the attachment
entirely.


<!-- source: agent-docs/interfaces-and-tooling.md -->

# Interfaces and tooling

## Turn context inspector

Each assistant message with a `turn_id` shows a "context" button
(`MessageDisplay.svelte:273`). Clicking it sets the reactive `inspectedTurnId`
and opens `TurnContextInspector.svelte`, which fetches
`GET /api/turns/{id}/context` (`handlers.rs:1239`, route at `server.rs:246`).

The endpoint reads a JSON snapshot from the `context_snapshots` table
(`turn_id TEXT PRIMARY KEY REFERENCES turns(id) ON DELETE CASCADE`,
`report_json TEXT NOT NULL`, `created_at TEXT NOT NULL`) and returns
`{ "turn_id": ..., "report": ... }`. 404 means no snapshot exists for that
turn.

The inspector panel displays:

| Section | Shown when | Content |
|---|---|---|
| Summary | Always | Assembly name, total tokens, element count, duration |
| Elements | Always | Table: element name, source (with optional preview), token count |
| Compaction | `compaction_applied` is non-empty | Element name, requested vs actual strategy, tokens before/after, messages removed |
| Fallbacks | `errors` is non-empty | Error message and which fallback assembly was used |
| Warnings | `warnings` is non-empty | Each warning string |

A `succession-degradation` compaction record's diagnosis details — the walls
answered, each model call (stage, model, usage, report), the synthesis text,
and the turn a reused diagnosis was originally written for — are held in the
turn's recorded context report, returned by `GET /api/turns/{id}/context`,
but are not rendered by the inspector panel. The report retains compaction
decisions from the first assembly and the successor in pass order, even when
their names match.

`AssemblyReport` and `TurnContextResponse` live in
`swage-protocol::client::context`. The stored-context endpoint and
`ContextAssembled` WebSocket event use the same typed report; the frontend
imports the generated `AssemblyReport.ts` projection.

The report's `provider_visible` object also records the resolved effort
for the turn (see [Agents and permissions — Effort](agents-and-permissions.md#effort)):
what was requested, what the adapter sent, and any clamp or substitution.
This data is stored in the report JSON but is not yet rendered by the
web UI's inspector panel; it is available through the
`GET /api/turns/{id}/context` endpoint.

`swage-tui` has a terminal-UI equivalent (`ui/inspector.rs:64`), toggled by
keybinding. It shows per-element fill bars and a budget percentage.

## Turn identity in streamed messages

The `turn_complete` WebSocket event carries the turn's `turn_id`
(`client/websocket.rs:134`). The streaming store passes it to
`conversationStore.appendAssistantMessage` at turn-complete
(`streaming.ts:256`), which merges it into the persisted message object
(`conversations.ts:90`). This lets the context-inspector button appear on a
just-completed message without a surface reload — the `turn_id` guard at
`MessageDisplay.svelte:273` matches live messages and API-loaded messages
alike.

The `RouterOptions.conversationStore` interface (`router.ts:47`) is a
four-member contract — `activeConversationId`, `checkConversationExists`,
`clearActiveConversation`, `selectConversation` — decoupled from Svelte store
internals.

## Conversation branching

A conversation can be branched from any message. The conversation's detail
carries a `root_thread_id` — the thread it started on — and its `messages`
are that thread's messages. A branch is a sibling thread
(`ConversationBranchResponse`) that carries the parent's messages up to the
message it was branched from, then diverges. A branch's messages are read
from `GET /api/threads/{id}` (`ConversationThreadDetail`).

### Routes

| Route | Method | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `/api/conversations/{id}/branches` | GET | List a conversation's branches (`ConversationBranchListResponse`) |
| `/api/conversations/{id}/branches` | POST | Branch at a message (`CreateConversationBranchRequest`: `thread_id`, `from_message_id`) → `ConversationBranchResponse` (201) |
| `/api/threads/{id}` | GET | Read one thread with its messages and, for a branch, its lineage |
| `/api/threads/{id}/abandon` | POST | Abandon a branch: it keeps its history and lineage but takes no further turns |

All four routes are in the client route manifest.

### Branch listing

Each `ConversationBranchResponse` carries `child_thread_id`,
`parent_thread_id`, `branched_from_message_id`, the
`branched_from_preview` (the opening of the branch-point message, absent
when that message no longer exists), and the thread's `state`.

### Thread states

A thread's `state` is one of `idle`, `processing`, `interrupted`,
`completed`, or `abandoned`. Abandoning is terminal: the branch keeps its
history and lineage and refuses further turns.

### Message identity

Every `MessageView` carries its own `id` and `thread_id`. The `id` is what
a branch is taken from (`from_message_id` in the branch request).

### Audit

Both branching and abandoning land in the session's audit trail.

## Image attachments

A message may carry content parts beside its text, submitted as the
`attachments` array on `SubmitTurnRequest` (REST) or the `SendMessage`
WebSocket event. Each attachment is a tagged `MessageAttachment`
(`swage-protocol::client::turn`); the only kind at this tree is `image_url`,
carrying a URL (https or `data:` inline).

### Intake check

`check_attachment_support` (`turn.rs:158`) runs before anything is persisted.
For each attachment:

1. An `image_url` with an empty URL is rejected as a `ValidationError`.
2. An `image_url` when the configured provider's `WorkflowCapabilities.vision()`
   is `false` is rejected as a `ValidationError`.
3. An `image_url` whose URL the provider cannot resolve — checked by
   `WorkflowCapabilities::accepts_image_reference` — is rejected as a
   `ValidationError` with a message advising a base64 `data:` URL instead.

Step 3 is the per-reference gate: vision support alone does not admit every
URL form. The check runs before the turn is persisted, so an unusable
reference never reaches the database or the provider.

### Which protocols claim vision

`WorkflowCapabilities::for_protocol` (`capabilities.rs:51`) sets the
`images` field per protocol. `vision()` returns `true` when `images` is
`Some`. The `images` value also determines which URL forms the intake gate
accepts:

| Protocol | Vision | Image references | Wire shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| `OpenAi` (Chat Completions) | Yes | `AnyUrl` — any `https` or `data:` URL | Typed content-part array: `{"type":"image_url","image_url":{"url":"…"}}` |
| `OpenRouter` | Yes | `AnyUrl` | Same Chat Completions adapter |
| `OpenAiResponses` (Responses) | Yes | `AnyUrl` | `{"type":"input_image","image_url":"…"}` |
| `Anthropic` | Yes | `AnyUrl` | `{"type":"image","source":{"type":"url","url":"…"}}` for URLs; `{"type":"image","source":{"type":"base64","media_type":"…","data":"…"}}` for `data:` URLs |
| `Google` | Yes | `InlineOrHostedFile` — `data:` URLs (carried as `inlineData`) and Google File API URIs (`https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/…`, carried as `fileData.fileUri`); arbitrary web URLs are refused at intake | `inlineData` blob or `fileData` reference |
| `Codex` | No | — | App Server integration; assembled text only |

Vision is claimed only where the adapter's message conversion maps
`ContentPart::ImageUrl` to the wire body. The capability is resolved once at
startup from the default provider's protocol and stored in
`AppState.workflow_capabilities`.

### Storage

Stored messages carry attachments as opaque JSON in the `attachments`
column of the `messages` table (`TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]'`). The
`MessageView` returned by the API includes the `attachments` array.
Text-only messages keep the plain string form on the wire; messages with
image parts use the provider-specific typed content array.

## Provider credentials

A provider entry in `config.toml` has two credential fields
(`ProviderEndpointConfig` in `swage-config/src/model.rs`):

| Field | Resolution | Audit/redaction |
|---|---|---|
| `api_key_secret_ref` | Resolved through the `SecretManager` by reference (`secret://{backend}/{id}`) with an audit event per access and the value registered for redaction | Yes |
| `api_key_env` | Direct `std::env::var` read at startup; legacy path, warned at startup (`startup.rs:449`) | No |

`resolve_provider_config` (`startup.rs:420`) checks `api_key_secret_ref`
first; if absent, falls back to `api_key_env`. The resolved secret must have
`material_kind` `"provider_key"`.

### Secret manager and backends

The `SecretManager` (`secret.rs`) resolves secrets by their `secret://`
reference, with an audit event per access and the resolved value registered
for redaction. A secret's `backend_kind` names where its value lives;
resolution reads the backend on every call, so material that changes
underneath is current at the next access.

| Backend | `backend_kind` | Value source |
|---|---|---|
| Managed | `managed` | Encrypted at rest in the gateway's SQLite store |
| Environment | `env` | `external_reference` names an environment variable |
| File | `file` | `external_reference` names a file path; `metadata.json_pointer` (RFC 6901) optionally selects one field of a JSON document |

### File backend

The file is re-read on every resolution. When `json_pointer` is absent, the
whole file (trimmed) is the value. When present, the file is parsed as JSON
and the pointer selects the field — a string value is used directly; any
other JSON type is serialised. The file's modification time is recorded as
the observation stamp.

### Registering a file-backed secret

Create the secret with `POST /api/secrets` (`server.rs:251`):

```json
{
  "name": "my-service-token",
  "material_kind": "provider_key",
  "owner_kind": "operator",
  "backend_kind": "file",
  "scope_kind": "provider",
  "scope_id": "my-provider",
  "external_reference": "/path/to/token-file.json",
  "metadata": { "json_pointer": "/tokens/access_token" }
}
```

The request fields (`CreateSecretRequest` in `secret.rs:43`):

| Field | Required | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `name` | Yes | Human-readable label |
| `material_kind` | Yes | What the secret is — `"provider_key"` for provider credentials |
| `owner_kind` | Yes | Who owns it — `"operator"`, `"harness"`, etc. |
| `backend_kind` | Yes | `"file"`, `"env"`, or `"managed"` |
| `scope_kind` | Yes | Scope category — `"provider"`, `"global"`, etc. |
| `scope_id` | No | Scope within the category |
| `external_reference` | No | File path (for `file`) or env var name (for `env`) |
| `metadata` | No | Backend-specific; `{"json_pointer": "..."}` for `file` |
| `value` | No | The secret material (for `managed` backend) |

The response includes a `reference` field (`secret://file/{id}`). Point the
provider entry's `api_key_secret_ref` at this reference:

```toml
[providers.entries.my-provider]
protocol = "openai"
api_key_secret_ref = "secret://file/<returned-id>"
```

### Codex auth store registration

At startup (`startup.rs:208`) the gateway registers the Codex CLI's
`auth.json` under the file backend as two records:

| Name | Material kind | JSON pointer |
|---|---|---|
| `codex.access_token` | `oauth_access_token` | `/tokens/access_token` |
| `codex.refresh_token` | `oauth_refresh_token` | `/tokens/refresh_token` |

Registration is idempotent: an existing active record for either token is
re-pointed at the current path. Registration precedes sign-in, so the file
need not exist yet. Both tokens resolve, audit, and redact through the
governed system.

## Surfaces

Surfaces are a session's work surfaces, assembled from ordered module
instances. Each surface belongs to one session (`session_id` on
`SurfaceResponse`; `sessions.session_id` in storage, cascading with the
session) and carries its own module list, annotations, and provenance.
`GET/POST /api/sessions/{session_id}/surfaces` list and create a session's
surfaces.

### The shared library

`POST /api/surfaces/{surface_id}/save` (`SaveSurfaceToLibraryRequest`: `name`,
`description`, `tags`) copies a surface's modules into a library entry and
records the origin topic (`origin_topic_id`, absent for the general scope).
The description is required — it is what an agent chooses by.
`GET /api/surface-library?tag=` is the catalogue (`LibraryListResponse`:
names, descriptions, tags, origin; no module content);
`GET /api/surface-library/{entry_id}` reads an entry with its module rows;
`DELETE` removes it, leaving surfaces added from it untouched.

Creating a surface with `library_entry_id` set seeds it from the entry
(`library_entry_id`, `seeded_at`, and `seeded_from_name` on
`SurfaceResponse`). Seeding carries the saved content only when the
session's topic is the entry's origin (`LibrarySeeding::WithContent`); any
other topic or the general scope receives the shape with empty modules
(`ShapeOnly`). The audit event `surface_created` records which under
`seeded_from.seeding`. The `seeded_from_name` persists even after the
library entry it was seeded from is deleted.

`GET/POST /api/topics/{topic_id}/default-surfaces` and
`DELETE /api/topics/{topic_id}/default-surfaces/{entry_id}` manage a topic's
default entries; the gateway opens them in every person-opened session of
the topic (sessions with origin `direct`). Schedule runs and other
automated sessions do not open default surfaces, and the general scope
designates no defaults. `topics.tags` (`UpdateTopicRequest.tags`) are the
labels the `surface_library` tool narrows the catalogue by for a topic's
sessions.

Library entries carry an `origin_topic_deleted` boolean, set when the entry's
origin topic is deleted. Deleting a topic keeps the entries saved from it
and other topics' default designations of those entries intact — the
catalogue marks the origin as deleted (`origin_topic_deleted: true`), and a
surface seeded from such an entry carries its shape only, because the
entry's content travels to no session once its origin topic is gone.

A save or delete broadcasts `ServerEvent::LibraryUpdated { entry_id }` on
the work-surface channel (`/api/work-surface/ws`), delivered like
`surface_updated`: identity only, no content. The frontend's surfaces store
answers it by refetching the catalogue, so the library page
(`/library`, `SurfaceLibrary.svelte`) and the surfaces pane's picker show a
new entry without a reload. From a session the page adds an entry through
the ordinary create route and navigates to the new surface; from the front
door (no session) it is read-only.

### Annotations

Annotations are notes hung on individual modules of a surface, anchored at
module grain — there is no per-surface or intra-module positioning.
`CreateSurfaceAnnotationRequest` takes `module_id`, `body`, and optional
`tags`. `UpdateSurfaceAnnotationRequest` replaces body and tags together; the
displaced text survives in the surface's provenance trail.

Deleting an annotation returns `DeleteSurfaceAnnotationResponse { deleted:
true }`. The delete is permanent — there is no soft-delete or archive. The
surfaces pane (`SurfacesPane.svelte`) exposes create, update
(`store.updateAnnotation` → `PUT /api/surface-annotations/{id}`) and delete.

### Surface addresses

`/conversations/{id}/surfaces/{surface_id}` (`Route.surfaceId`;
`conversationPath(id, surfaceId)` in `router.ts`) addresses an open surface.
`SurfacesPane` opens the routed surface once the session's list is loaded
and reports the surface the user opens (`onOpenSurface`) so the shell keeps
the URL in step; a deep link or Back restores the surface with the session.

### Work-surface reconnect

When a WebSocket connection to a surface's work surface drops and reconnects,
the frontend refetches the surface state to pick up any writes that landed
while disconnected. `library_updated` rides the same channel and refetches
the catalogue.

## Workspace relinking

When a workspace directory moves on disk, the attachment can be relinked to
its new path without detaching and re-attaching:
`PUT /api/topics/{topic_id}/workspaces/{workspace_id}/relink`
(`RelinkWorkspaceAttachmentRequest`: `path`). Relinking updates only the
path and clears the missing flag; the attachment's label, configured
permissions, trust state, and default status are preserved.

## Delivery targets

A run's output can be routed to one or more destinations through
`DeliveryRoutingRequest` (`swage-protocol::client::delivery`). The four
target kinds:

| Kind | Fields | Destination |
|---|---|---|
| `channel` | `integration`, `account`, `conversation` | An external channel (Telegram, dev DM/thread) |
| `local_storage` | — | The gateway's local store, as a log record |
| `surface` | `surface_id` | A surface owned by the continuing session (schedules) or by a session in the run's topic (workflows) |
| `webhook` | `url` | An HTTP endpoint |

`store_local_output` on the routing request adds a `local_storage` target
alongside any explicit targets, so the output is always retained locally
when set.

### No-delivery records

When a schedule run produces no output delivery, the channel gateway
records a no-delivery entry (`record_no_delivery`,
`channel_gateway.rs:777`) with target `{"kind": "no_delivery"}`, status
`"not_delivered"`, and the reason as the error field. Three outcomes
produce this record:

| Outcome | Run state | Reason recorded |
|---|---|---|
| Gate skip | `skipped` (`skip_reason: gate`) | The gate model's message, or "schedule gate decided no work was needed" |
| Overlap skip | `skipped` (`skip_reason: overlap`) | "schedule run overlapped an in-flight run" |
| Failure before delivery | `failed` (`error_message` set) | The failure message from the run body |

`SkipReason` (`swage-protocol::client::schedule`) is the enum behind the
first two. A run that fails after delivery has already been attempted does
not receive a no-delivery record — `delivery_attempted` on the failure
controls this (`schedule.rs:1267`).

## Devices

A device registers once, naming the gateway secret its credential resolves
against and the workspace it operates in, then dials into the gateway over
a persistent connection. Nothing listens on the device: the device opens the
connection, advertises what it can run, and the gateway invokes operations
back over the same socket. `swage device connect` runs a machine as a device.

### Registration and pairing

A device can join in two ways:

- **Direct registration** — `POST /api/devices/register`
  (`RegisterDeviceRequest` in `swage-protocol::device`). The caller supplies
  the device identity, the gateway secret its credential resolves against,
  and the workspace it operates in.
- **Pairing** — the gateway issues a one-time pairing code
  (`POST /api/onboarding/devices/pairing-codes`, with an optional
  `expires_in_seconds`; default 600 s), and the device redeems it
  (`POST /api/onboarding/devices/redeem` with the code and its registration
  fields) to register and trust itself in one step.

In both paths the `kind` field defaults to `"attached_device"` and names the
device type. A `kind` of `"local"` is refused with a `ValidationError`: a
local device has no remote producer to register. The same refusal applies to
recovery imports, so the remote-device registry never holds a local entry.
What a device can run is not registered — the device advertises its
capabilities each time it connects.

### The connection

The device dials `GET /api/devices/connect` (WebSocket). The handshake:

1. The device sends a `Hello` frame: `device_id`, `shared_token` (resolved
   against the secret named at registration), `label`, and `capabilities`
   (the tools it can run).
2. The gateway validates the credential and answers `Welcome` (with
   `heartbeat_interval_secs`) or `Rejected` (with a message) and closes.

After the welcome the connection carries two frame types in each direction:

| Direction | Frame | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| Gateway → device | `Operation` | Run `tool_name` with `params` in `context`; carries a `correlation_id` |
| Gateway → device | `Cancel` | Stop the operation `correlation_id` if still running |
| Device → gateway | `Result` | Operation `correlation_id` finished with `output` |
| Device → gateway | `Failure` | Operation `correlation_id` failed with `message` |
| Device → gateway | `Cancelled` | Operation `correlation_id` was stopped |
| Device → gateway | `Heartbeat` | Sent every `heartbeat_interval_secs` (default 10 s) |

All frames are tagged by `kind` (snake_case) and defined in
`swage-protocol::device` (`DeviceFrame`, `GatewayFrame`).

### Cancellation

When a turn is cancelled, the gateway sends `Cancel` for each in-flight
device operation. For local shell commands (`shell` tool), cancellation
kills the entire process group (`SIGKILL` to `-pid`), stopping the command
and all its descendants.

### Presence

Presence begins when the gateway accepts the device's hello: the gateway
records a heartbeat at the accepted hello, marking the device `connected`
before the welcome is sent. Subsequent heartbeats (sent every
`heartbeat_interval_secs`, default 10 s, as the welcome tells the device)
keep the device connected. The gateway marks a device `stale` after 3× the
heartbeat interval without a heartbeat, and `disconnected` when the
WebSocket closes.

The operator can close a device's connection from the gateway side with
`DELETE /api/presence/devices/{id}`, which disconnects the device and marks
it disconnected.

Every connect, disconnect, invocation, and settlement lands in the audit
trail under the device's id.

## Wire error contract

Every failed HTTP response on the client surface carries
`{"code":"<snake_case>","message":"…"}` — the `ApiErrorBody` type
(`swage-protocol::client::error`).

### ErrorCode enum

`ErrorCode` (`error.rs:21`) names one HTTP status each:

| Code | Status | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `malformed_body` | 400 | Body was not valid JSON or could not be read |
| `forbidden` | 403 | Caller may not perform this operation |
| `not_found` | 404 | Addressed entity does not exist |
| `conflict` | 409 | Collides with existing state |
| `turn_in_progress` | 409 | Conversation already has a turn in flight |
| `already_connected` | 409 | Conversation already has a live connection |
| `unsupported_media_type` | 415 | Missing `Content-Type: application/json` |
| `validation_error` | 422 | Body parsed but failed validation |
| `sign_in_unsupported` | 422 | Provider offers no sign-in flow of the requested kind |
| `internal_error` | 500 | Unexpected gateway failure |
| `provider_error` | 502 | Upstream model provider failed |
| `sign_in_failed` | 502 | Provider refused or could not complete sign-in |
| `provider_runtime_unavailable` | 503 | Provider runtime could not be started or reached |

The HTTP status is a projection of the code (`ErrorCode::status`), never an
independent fact. Codes serialise as `snake_case` strings via serde.

### Coverage

`GatewayError` maps exhaustively to an `ErrorCode` — a new variant must
choose one. The gateway's own `Json` extractor answers body-parsing
rejections (malformed JSON, unsupported media type, `deny_unknown_fields`
violations naming the rejected field) in the same `ApiErrorBody` shape.
Handlers construct refusals through `ApiError` rather than hand-built bodies.

### Client consumers

- **Rust client** — `ClientError::Gateway` variant parses the body into a
  typed error.
- **Frontend** — `ApiError` class (`frontend/src/lib/api/error.ts`) reads
  the `code` field. The generated TypeScript client's request helper raises
  `ApiError` on non-ok responses.

## Wire-contract architecture

All types that cross a process boundary live in `swage-protocol`
(`crates/swage-protocol/`). Gateway modules consume or re-export those Rust
types, and frontend wire types come from generated projections under
`frontend/src/lib/protocol/`.

The crate is organised into four surface modules:

| Surface | Module | Anchor type | Scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| Client | `src/client/` | `ClientSurface` | Conversations, streaming, approvals, schedules, knowledge, voice, workflows, channels, delivery, topics, settings, materials, recovery, context reports, provider sign-in |
| Hosting | `src/hosting.rs` | `HostingSurface` | Presence, operator overview, agent definitions, approvals, configuration |
| Device | `src/device.rs` | `DeviceSurface` | Device registration, remote tool execution |
| Channel | `src/channel.rs` | `ChannelSurface` | Inbound messages (DM/thread), delivery log, channel status |

Each manually maintained anchor struct must reference every wire type on its
surface. A `schemars::schema_for!` call walks only the type graph reachable from
that anchor, so a new top-level type must be added to the anchor unless an
existing field already reaches it.

### Route manifest

`routes.rs` (`swage-protocol::client::routes`) carries a growing manifest of
client-surface HTTP routes: method, path template, path parameters, request
body schema name, and response body schema name. The manifest does not yet
cover the full client surface — the topic CRUD routes are the first entries;
routes not yet in the manifest are registered directly on the router and are
not covered by the OpenAPI or generated-client projections. Failures are not
listed per route — every route answers a failure with `ApiErrorBody`,
projected once as the shared error response.

Adding a manifested route is one entry in the `routes()` function; the
OpenAPI document, the generated TypeScript client, and the router-coverage
test all read this table. The router test (`server.rs:418`) proves every
manifest route is registered on the axum router — a manifest entry with no
matching handler fails the test.

### Projections

| Projection | Output | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| TypeScript types (ts-rs) | `frontend/src/lib/protocol/` | `projections.rs` test manually calls `export_all` for each top-level export, then trims trailing whitespace |
| JSON Schema (schemars) | `crates/swage-protocol/schema/{client,hosting,device,channel}.json` | `projections.rs` tests per surface, via the anchor type |
| OpenAPI 3.1 (from route manifest) | `crates/swage-protocol/schema/client-openapi.json` | `projections.rs` test renders `openapi::document()`, which walks the manifest and reuses the client surface's JSON Schema as its `components/schemas` |
| TypeScript client (from route manifest) | `frontend/src/lib/protocol/client.ts` | `projections.rs` test renders `typescript_client::generate()` — one typed function per manifest route over a shared `request` helper that raises `ApiError` on non-ok responses |

Running `cargo test -p swage-protocol` regenerates all projections in place.
New top-level wire types must be added to the appropriate anchor for JSON
Schema and to the explicit `export_all` list for TypeScript unless already
reachable from an existing entry. New routes must be added to the `routes()`
manifest for the OpenAPI and client projections. Drift shows as uncommitted
changes, caught by the verify gate's projection-freshness check; an
unregistered type or unmanifested route creates no drift for that check to
detect.

## Verification gate

`xtask` (`xtask/src/main.rs`) orchestrates the verification gate; the
`Justfile` is a thin dispatch into `cargo run -p xtask -- <subcommand>`.
Most logic is Rust, but `xtask` shells out for some checks (e.g.
`scripts/check-tracked-local-state.sh`).

### Recipes

| Recipe | What it runs |
|---|---|
| `just check-gate` | Tracked-local-state, format, Rust/frontend type, frontend design-token, and clippy checks; no tests |
| `just check` | `cargo check --workspace` + frontend type check (`npm run check`) |
| `just test` | Full test suite with failure aggregation (see below) |
| `just verify` (alias: `just ci`) | `check-gate`, then the test and projection stages below; the gate CI runs |

### Verify stages

`check-gate` runs stages 1--5 and aborts on the first failure (`?` operator).
Stages 6--7 run regardless; their results are combined.

| # | Stage | Short-circuits? |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Tracked-local-state check (`scripts/check-tracked-local-state.sh`) | Yes |
| 2 | Format check (`cargo fmt --all -- --check` + `just --fmt --check`) | Yes |
| 3 | Type check (`cargo check --workspace` + frontend) | Yes |
| 4 | Frontend design-token check | Yes |
| 5 | Clippy (`-D warnings`) | Yes |
| 6 | Test suite (Rust with `--no-fail-fast`, frontend, desktop smoke) | No |
| 7 | Projection freshness (`git diff --exit-code` on generated files) | No |

When both tests and projections fail, both errors surface in one message.
The test suite aggregates Rust, frontend, and desktop-smoke failures into a
`Vec<String>` rather than aborting on the first.

The verify body runs inside `run_with_final_sweep`, which runs
`cargo sweep` after the gate (even on failure) and reports the artefact
budget.

## Client-side route preservation

The SPA router (`frontend/src/lib/router.ts`) is framework-free: `parseRoute`
pattern-matches the URL (`/`, `/conversations/{id}`,
`/conversations/{id}/surfaces/{surface_id}`, `/library`,
`/workflow-runs/{id}`, `/settings/...`, `/settings/topic/{slug}/...`);
`createRouter` manages `pushState` navigation and `popstate` listening.

`applyLocation()` runs on every URL change. When the URL contains a
conversation ID:

- **Already active:** calls `checkConversationExists` — a lightweight `GET`
  that confirms the conversation exists without re-fetching it. On 404,
  clears the active conversation and falls back to root with a not-found
  notice. On transient failure (non-404), the conversation is kept and the
  error is swallowed.
- **Different conversation:** calls `selectConversation`, which fully loads
  it. On 404, falls back to root. On other errors, the error propagates.

The `conversationStore` dependency is injected as a four-member interface,
wired in `App.svelte`. `clearActiveConversation` disconnects the WebSocket
before clearing the store, preventing orphaned connections.

Route changes propagate `notFound` state to the UI, so the "conversation not
found" notice appears for `popstate`-triggered navigations and initial surface
loads alike. When a scope was in view, `App.svelte` keeps a pending start in
it (the composer stays open; the next message creates a session there);
otherwise the front door serves.

Session creation is fenced against a scope change: `createAndNavigate`
captures a scope generation before the request and hands the store a
`shouldInstall` check, so a session created for one scope is neither listed
nor activated once the user has moved to another (it exists in the scope it
was asked for, and the recent list finds it).

## Tool-call recording and replay

Tool calls are recorded in two phases. A record is created when the model
selects the tool call (`create_tool_call`), before execution begins. Once
execution completes, the record is settled with the result
(`update_tool_call_result`). This means a tool call that was selected but
never finished — interrupted by cancellation, a crash, or a turn that ended
before the result could be recorded — has a record with no result.

At turn startup, unsettled tool calls from a prior interrupted turn are
replayed into the conversation history so the model sees what happened.
Completed tool calls replay with their recorded results. A tool call that
was interrupted or whose result could not be recorded replays with an
explicit unknown-outcome text rather than replaying as though it returned
successfully:

- An interrupted call (no result, no status): `"tool call did not report a
  result; its outcome is unknown"` with status `"interrupted"`.
- A call that ran but whose result could not be recorded: `"tool call ran,
  but its result could not be recorded"` with status `"result_unavailable"`.

When a tool-call result cannot be recorded (the settlement write fails),
the turn ends as `Failed` — the result is not silently dropped.

## Hosted documentation

The gateway compiles the agent-facing documentation set (`agent-docs/`) into
the binary (`crate::shipped_docs`) and serves it read-only. Documents are
addressed by name — the file stem of the source under `agent-docs/`. The set
is flat: no subdirectories.

| Route | Response |
|---|---|
| `GET /api/docs` | `DocumentListResponse`: each document's `name`, `title`, and `description` |
| `GET /api/docs/{name}` | `DocumentResponse`: the document's Markdown body, front matter included |

Both routes are in the client route manifest (`swage-protocol::client::docs`).

The `docs_read` tool (`tool/docs_read.rs`) exposes this to agents: call with
no arguments to list the documents with descriptions; call with a `name` to
read one. A document longer than the tool's output limit pages by byte offset
(`offset_bytes`), the same continuation shape `url_fetch` uses. The tool
executes in the gateway process (`requires_device_execution: true`).

The `catalogue_embeds_every_document_byte_for_byte` test
(`swage-gateway::shipped_docs`) proves each compiled document is
byte-identical to the repository source. The
`every_shipped_document_carries_a_title_and_description` test verifies the
metadata the listing returns.

## Voice capabilities

`GET /api/voice/capabilities` returns a `VoiceCapabilitiesResponse`
(`swage-protocol::client::voice`):

| Field | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `transcription` | bool | Whether speech-to-text is available |
| `synthesis` | bool | Whether text-to-speech is available |
| `default_voice` | string or null | The default synthesis voice (e.g. `"alloy"`) |
| `supported_voices` | string[] | Available synthesis voices |
| `unavailable_reason` | string or null | What to configure to enable a missing capability; absent when both are available |

The `unavailable_reason` names the unset `[voice]` keys — e.g.
"set `transcription_model` and `speech_model` in the [voice] settings to a
model the default provider serves". See
[Agents and permissions — Voice configuration](agents-and-permissions.md#voice-configuration)
for the configuration keys.

The voice routes (`/api/voice/transcribe`, `/api/voice/synthesise`) use the
configured model ids against the default provider's OpenAI-protocol audio
endpoints. A request to an unavailable capability returns a 422 validation
error.

## Gateway tools

The gateway ships these built-in tools
(`crates/swage-gateway/src/tool/`). A tool's `requires_device_execution`
flag (`swage-tool::Tool` trait) determines whether it executes in the
gateway process or can run through the bubblewrap sandbox: `true` means
the tool must execute in the gateway process (bypassing the sandbox);
`false` (the trait default) means it is eligible for sandboxed execution.
All built-in tools set `true` except `shell` and `memory`, which are the
two sandbox-eligible tools.
